details:
**The Stranger (Meursault)**
Camus's most famous novel (1942), narrated by the emotionally detached French-Algerian clerk Meursault. He shoots an unnamed Arab on a beach in Algiers, blaming the blinding sun, and at his trial he is condemned less for the killing than for his lack of feeling, especially for not crying at his mother's funeral.

**"Maman died today"**
The famous opening line of The Stranger, also translated "Mother died today." Meursault attends his mother's vigil and funeral at a nursing home in Marengo, smoking and drinking coffee beside the coffin, which the prosecution later uses against him.

**The Plague (Dr. Bernard Rieux and Oran)**
Camus's 1947 novel about an outbreak of bubonic plague that quarantines the Algerian city of Oran, beginning when thousands of rats die in the streets. Dr. Bernard Rieux leads the fight against the disease and turns out to be the novel's narrator, revealing himself only near the end because he wants the account to be objective.

**Father Paneloux**
The Jesuit priest in The Plague who preaches that the epidemic is God's punishment, telling the townspeople, "Calamity has come on you, my brethren, and, my brethren, you deserved it." After watching the agonizing death of Judge Othon's young son, he gives a second, humbler sermon. When he dies, his record card reads "Doubtful case."

**Tarrou, Cottard, Rambert, and Grand**
Other characters in The Plague. Jean Tarrou keeps notebooks (including notes on an old man who drops scraps of paper from his balcony to lure cats, then spits on them) and organizes sanitary squads. Cottard profits by smuggling during the quarantine and ends up firing a gun at people from his apartment. The journalist Raymond Rambert tries to escape to his lover in Paris but stays to help, and the clerk Joseph Grand endlessly rewrites the first sentence of his novel.

**The Fall (Jean-Baptiste Clamence)**
Camus's 1956 novel, a series of dramatic monologues spoken by Jean-Baptiste Clamence, a once-successful Parisian defense lawyer who calls himself a "judge-penitent." He confesses his hypocrisy to an unseen listener and compares the concentric canals of Amsterdam to the circles of hell.

**The Mexico City bar and The Just Judges**
Clamence holds court at a seedy Amsterdam bar called Mexico City. He keeps the stolen "Just Judges" panel of Jan van Eyck's Ghent Altarpiece hidden in a cupboard in his apartment.

**The woman on the bridge**
The turning point of Clamence's life in The Fall: one night in Paris he crossed a bridge, heard a young woman throw herself into the Seine, and did nothing to save her. Another humiliation he recalls is being struck by a motorcyclist in an argument and failing to hit back.

**Salamano and his dog**
Meursault's elderly neighbor in The Stranger, who constantly beats and curses his mangy spaniel, which is covered in scabs. When the dog runs away at a fair, Salamano is grief-stricken.

**Raymond Sintes**
Meursault's neighbor in The Stranger, a pimp who asks Meursault to write a letter luring back his Arab mistress so he can punish her. The conflict with her brother and his friends leads to the confrontation on the beach where Meursault kills the Arab, and Raymond later testifies for Meursault at the trial.

**"The benign indifference of the universe"**
The ending of The Stranger. After angrily rejecting the prison chaplain's offer of faith, Meursault opens himself to the "gentle" or "benign indifference" of the world and feels happy, hoping for a large crowd at his execution to greet him with cries of hate. His girlfriend Marie Cardona and the restaurant owner Céleste appear earlier in the novel.

**Exile and the Kingdom**
Camus's 1957 collection of six short stories. It includes "The Adulterous Woman" (Janine, unhappily married to Marcel, slips out at night to a fort overlooking the desert), "The Renegade" (a missionary whose tongue is cut out by the tribe he tried to convert), "The Silent Men," and "Jonas, or the Artist at Work" (about a painter who loses his ability to paint).

**"The Growing Stone"**
The last story of Exile and the Kingdom. The French engineer d'Arrast comes to Iguape, Brazil, to build a sea wall and meets a ship's cook who vowed to carry a huge stone to the church in a procession. When the cook collapses, d'Arrast carries the stone himself but takes it to the cook's hut instead of the church.

**"The Guest"**
A story in Exile and the Kingdom set in Algeria. The gendarme Balducci delivers an Arab prisoner to Daru, a schoolteacher in the mountains, who refuses to hand him over and instead leaves him free to choose between prison and escape.

**The Myth of Sisyphus**
Camus's 1942 philosophical essay laying out the absurd: the conflict between humanity's search for meaning and a silent universe. He rejects suicide in favor of revolt, using Sisyphus endlessly rolling his boulder as a model and concluding that "one must imagine Sisyphus happy." Other works include the posthumous novels A Happy Death and The First Man, and the play The Just Assassins.
